name: Carrow & Sons Waxed Drover Coat
description:
A full-length waxed cotton drover coat in dark tobacco or midnight green, cut long enough to cover the knee and wide enough to layer over a sweater or light armor. The silhouette is unapologetically traditional — storm collar, deep side-entry pockets, a back vent for riding or climbing. The wax finish sheds rain without membrane technology, just good old-fashioned textile chemistry applied to a tight-woven cotton canvas. It smells faintly of beeswax and machine oil.

Carrow & Sons has been operating out of a warehouse-district workshop in the Tier 2 belt since 2161. The coat is heavy, stiff when new, and breaks in over years of wear. Dock workers, outer-district beat cops, and stubborn middle-class types who distrust smart-fabric all wear it. It gets better with age in a way synthetic jackets never do.
what_it_says: You value durability over novelty. You've probably owned this coat for a decade and plan to own it for two more.
story_hooks: A dockworker's coat has a bloodstain on the inner lining that its current owner didn't put there — and the previous owner has been missing for three months.
Carrow & Sons is being bought out by a Tier 4 corponation that wants to move manufacturing offsite; the founding family is quietly sabotaging the deal.
The coat's wax formula is apparently based on a proprietary compound that a street chemist claims is being used in a very different product.

physical_description.visual_profile: A substantial, floor-grazing overcoat with a distinctly analog aesthetic. The silhouette is broad-shouldered and generous through the body, evoking early 21st-century workwear rather than contemporary synthfabric fashion. Knee-length cut creates an imposing, authoritative presence on the wearer.
physical_description.fit: Intentionally oversized and relaxed through the torso to accommodate layering. Sleeves are long and straight. The storm collar sits high and structured. Cut to allow freedom of movement for physical labor or climbing.
physical_description.primary_material: Heavy waxed cotton canvas, tight-weave construction. Untreated, non-responsive textile — no embedded circuitry or smart fibers.
physical_description.texture: Waxy surface with visible weave texture beneath. Starts stiff and glossy, develops subtle creasing and a matte patina with age. Faintly tacky to touch when new. Visible beeswax bloom on seams.
physical_description.color_scheme: Deep tobacco brown or midnight green, depending on batch. Both colorways age to warmer, grayer tones. No pattern; solid, earthy finish. Darker wax accumulation visible along stress points after months of wear.
physical_description.closures: Five substantial bone or aged-brass buttons down the front. Button-through storm flap over the collar. No magnetic fasteners or friction-locks.
distinctive_features: Deep side-entry pockets large enough for tools or ammunition
Center back vent with hidden buttons for riding/climbing mobility
Hand-stitched seams with visible wax saturation
Carrow & Sons woven label on interior left breast
Deliberately visible wear and age patina on older examples
Faint beeswax and machine-oil scent that persists through seasons
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 2-3 crossover. Expensive enough to signal deliberate craftsmanship and resistance to trend, but worn by working-class and mid-tier professionals who value durability over status.
physical_description.cultural_context: Worn by dock workers, outer-district beat cops, salvage operators, and analog-preference professionals. Signals skepticism of corpo smart-fabric culture, self-reliance, and distrust of technology dependency. Associated with the warehouse districts and pre-Expansion sensibilities.
physical_description.condition_typical: Breaks in over 2-3 years. Newer coats appear stiff and overly shiny. Well-worn examples develop creases, darkened stress points, and a softer, more supple surface. Patching is common; owners repair rather than replace.

Rain-slicked fabric catches amber light. Model has visible augmentations (chrome wrist, subdermal implant scar) to contrast the analog garment.
